text: everything can be stopped and nothing can be done and this is the crisis fundamentally of the modern state to a large extent and it is the result of the disappearance of the great issues that divided us in the past and it is a don't see the answer now what follows from this for management let me see I believe that in a very difficult time and I think we are back to normal which is turbulent times smooth sailing is not normal management will have to think through how to create well responsibility in the workforces in the sense that the relationship I'm not saying identity that's the relationship between the welfare of both the enterprise and the economy and that of the employee is institutionalized. What the organs are, I don't know. Whether they're internal, where I think with the labor forces we have now, the personnel policies we follow in which we try to do as much as possible for the employee are becoming self-defeating. Or whether it is through trying to bring the employee interest in the ownership of the enterprise and in its long range success, which is organized around the pension plan, whether that becomes an institutional basis exercised through a far more powerful board of directors. These are all possibilities, but I think it is need to go to work inside and outside. I think there is need for organized schizophrenia. Now what we have today is disorganized one and I don't think that's tenable. Organized one is difficult because on the one hand this society is ready for a group that has competence to assert its responsibility for the common weal. I'm impressed, as you know, by a few of the things the Japanese are doing, and nothing impressed me more than a call about what I think two days after I came home from my last meeting here in April, I got the call from Tokyo, seeing the chief executive officers of the 25 largest Japanese companies will be in the West and want to spend a week with you thinking through what is the right national policy for Japan, considering the change in demographics. And when I sat down with them, I said, uh have you thought through what you're in business want to do and should do and just said with one voice that is the wrong place to start that comes second what is right for japan because we have to give leadership and then we think through how they we fit in mitsubishi and mitsui and sumitomo into the national policy and that has been long been the basic strengths of the Japanese and the reason why Japanese business mostly gets the policies it wants because it doesn't start out with the policies it wants. And I think we have to learn that in a society in which almost all traditional leadership groups have become the victims of factionalism, it is both an opportunity and a need for business leadership to speak for the producer interest in society especially at a time when we very clearly are going to shift from consumer dominated to producer I wouldn't say dominated but to economics that again realize that money doesn't grow on trees and productivity doesn't grow on trees and that the essence of economics is not to devise better ways of shaking the tree but better ways of growing it. And then I think the time is ripe for the producer interest to reassert itself as a national interest. and to think through and speak about national policies, and it's singularly lacking. Let me see if you want an example of what not to do, for which business is going to pay very dearly. In the last 10 years, since 1969 precisely, one and only two groups in society have had their incomes largely shielded against inflation. There were social security recipients and top management people. Top management people because of the 50% maximum tax on earned income. Everybody else, everybody who makes less than $100,000 1969 money, has seen his tax rate go up much faster than inflation. So anything that was done to protect his income against inflation was to a large extent offset by income tax ratcheting. You all know what I'm talking about. Except for the people who own more than $100,000 per family income, about half of whom are executives of business. The other half are doctors, lawyers, and so on. And I have yet to hear a single man in a senior executive position scream about the gross injustice and inequity to his associates. Ladies and gentlemen, that is frivolous irresponsibility, and we are going to pay very heavily for it. They all said, let's not rock the boat, because God forbid if we do, somebody nasty in Congress will say, let's repeal the maximum tax. And that risk was there, but one is paid to take these risks, and one cannot any longer duck them. And this is what I'm talking about. That is thinking through the responsibility as a national leader with competence, with a producer interest in one's charge. And at the same time, I think there is no doubt that business will have to organize, and is organizing, by the way, to become another faction. I loathe fashions. Everything said about fashions in the Federalist Papers is all too true. But neither you nor I are in control of the universe. Even in everyday, we are less in control of the universe. And then has to be able to survive. and if the streets are dominated by street gangs then one has to organize one's own with all the danger attendant there too let me say the mafia has its origin in legitimate need for protection and it degenerated pretty fast, a couple of hundred years but it was a survival necessity necessarily mismanaged by every invader And so one has to organize in a new fashion and use one's veto power to block things. So business, I think, in this new political environment has two quite different tasks, or three. The task of creating a constituency again. Most of the things I see you do in your public relations, in your lobbying, are simply futile. They assume that you have that small business constituency in Main Street. That constituency is gone, and your engineers and your accountants have not taken its place, and you have to organize, except the fact that 90% of most old Americans today are employees, and that 90-plus percent or more educated people are employees. One goes to school to get the job with General Foods. One doesn't go to school to be independent. And on the other hand, General Foods could not exist but for the fact that the schools use social society's money to train people for General Foods. General Foods wouldn't be able to pay their training expense. and you are still appealing to the corner druggist who even if he exists is simply such a tiny minority as to be meaningless but the only small businessmen that have political clout in state capitals are the undertakers the only effective lobby in California and their interests and ours fortunately do not run parallel. And so the rest are your employees, and especially your educated ones, and we have not built that constituency. We have not made overt the links and bonds we have with them, and that is a real, we have not given them responsibility, and nobody has learned, really understanding, without the responsibility and the chance to make mistakes. And then we have to learn that this is a nation badly in need of a voice it can trust, that is not starting out with we want, we need, but with the country the world needs, the country the world wants, badly need, because there is none today not the one and finally at the same time if the gangs and the toughs roam the street you better organize yourself and get a fairly potent weapon and learn how to operate as a faction and these are the requirements of a political environment that for better or worse I happen to to think it's for the worst, is not the environment of 1920, of 1930, and not even of 1950, but far more akin to the environment of 1740. If you want to understand politics, will you please not read 19th century political scientists? God help you, don't read 20th century ones. When only they're set to get a PhD. And will you go back to the 18th century? And if anybody's interested in political science, there's only one book today that a business leader should read to understand. It has a very peculiar title. It's called The Patriot King. It was written in 1736 in England. That's the only text for this time. We are back in the 18th century in politics. And we have to learn again how one behaves in such an environment so that we can rebuild a true political community. Thank you very much, ladies and gentlemen.

The one theoretical flaw in the Keynesian system who assumed it can only go one way. If there is no law, it can go either way, you know. If you don't assume that, it has to be either savings equals investment or there's over-savings. If you see there is no necessary correlation between the two, except that you can't have capital formation investment without savings, then you find that if you take what people consider savings, which is deferred consumption, you have about the same rates with one and only one independent variable, which is the age structure of the society. It makes sense, you know. And since all developed societies have roughly the same age structure, roughly, the Japanese now have the longest age, but that's a year and a half different. Other than that, we all have the same age structures and the same demographic structures. You get the same savings rates, they're only collected differently. A larger or greater part of the savings is available for investment and is not used for transfer payments into consumption. Thank you very much, Bob Hawkins. Let me apologize for not our inability to answer all questions. We would be here till about midnight and still not have finished with all of them. And in a way, I'm very glad that we have to cut it off because there are some I'm very happy I don't have to answer, such as the question from the lady from the New York Times, what kind of an executive will he need tomorrow? Let me say, let's face it, the kind of people who do have to do the job are exactly the kind of people we have now. Evolution isn't going to be that fast. The question is will you be able to think through your policy, your direction, and will you finally go to work on placing people where their strengths can produce results results instead of trying to either hope for a different breed, this human being isn't going to change very much, or making exaggerated expectations in respect to what education and development can produce. Believe me, the key to answering the demands of tomorrow is not different people or better people, which is unlikely to happen, but better place people, where their strengths can really redound to performance, and it is a neglected area of management is to think through what Joe Blow or Jane Doe can do, and to make sure he and she is allowed, permitted, expected to do it. So I don't believe we are going to see a major change in the human race or a major change in human qualifications. Neither of them are very rational expectations. The only way is to improve the yield of what we have, and that is putting people at very specific resources. No two individuals are alike. That is to spend a great deal of hard work and thinking on where individuals belong. And by the way, one question was, what do the Japanese do better than we in using people? Believe me, since they cannot fire anybody, they are forced to think much harder than we do where you place people. And in that respect, their immobility is an asset. and we are not using our mobility sufficiently as an asset because we are not thinking sufficiently where to place people, which is already an introduction to my topic, which is what we might learn from others. And I quite intentionally picked that topic because this series began 15 years ago, I think this is our 16th anniversary, with one that was caused, or really was a response, to Savant Schreiber's book on the American Challenge. We had the first series here, then in 65 or 64, I've forgotten, in which basically the conviction every place was that it was at the peak that we had invented management, which some of you know isn't true, And we have somehow the secret of management, which, God help us, isn't so easy. And somehow the others all the world over were organizing themselves very effectively to learn from us. And to a large extent, you can look upon the development of the post-war period as a diffusion of American management, not technology if you want to call it that, with people who were willing to look at us and say, what are these people doing that explains their effectiveness and in what way can we use it ourselves. The ones who tried to imitate us didn't get very far. Let me say that one of the weaknesses of my friends in Great Britain, in British industry, is that they are too Americanized in the sense that they are using things that came from this country, the old remark about two countries divided by a common language and simply slapped things on and they don't fit either their objective reality or their social and cultural tradition in many cases and so one of the things that is very clear is that where you see success in the United Kingdom It is very heavily built around people who were trained in and by American companies, who, however, then when they moved into a British company, thought how to adapt it, what fits and what doesn't, rather than copy it. And the great majority copied, and copies are weak. Carbon copies are weak, and they don't really become organic. And where you see results in these people who learned just the same thing, but did not copy, but then say, what does it mean for us and for me? And I'm going to talk about some things one can now learn from others who in the last 15 years have been relatively, and in some cases absolutely, more successful and more effective than we have been, but not to imitate, but to say how do we then make this part of our culture, our tradition, our structure, our policies. And if yesterday some of you were here, yesterday it was many, and you may remember Irving Kristol and you and I had a discussion about leadership and where we talked about the fact that in countries like especially Japan and Germany, The large, the major business leaders see themselves as responsible for thinking through what the right national policy would be in areas in which business leaders might be expected to have competence. And I cited the example of the visit I had a few months ago from a Japanese group, the chief executive officers of the 25 largest Japanese companies who came over here, to always have one question, what policy should we in Japan have in respect to retirement, wages, what have you, in view of our changing demographics? And when I said, now, what do you think is the right thing for business to do, I was sharply called to order by the chairman who said, that is the next question. The first question is, what's the right policy for Japan? Only when we know that do we even think about what the right policy is for our company. And that is a very different view of the role. And if you want to see where does it come from, it's root, like so much that is good, is in pure vice. It is basically in vanity in Japan and in Germany, where the businessman was basically not respected in what were, in both countries, bureaucratic traditions. You have an exaggerated, perhaps, desire on the part of the business leaders to be respectable and to be gentlemen, and to remove from that stigma of filthy lucre, and so they became pompous and statesmen. But it had also its desirable side effects. phenomenon is purely bad, the side effects are quite good. And one of them is that they realize how visible they are in today's world, and that one cannot be that visible without representing. And one of the things I think one has to learn is that in this world in which the old tradition, for better or worse of complete separation of the political and the economic no longer works and sometimes I wish the other Friedman Milton could prevail and we could restore that separation but I don't think one can restore virginity and this would be akin to it and I don't believe it works and so we have to accept that those two if they ever were that clean separated outside of the lecture halls of the University of Chicago and I have my doubts will never be separated again and then one has to say the heads of the large institutions not just businesses, are so visible. They are the only leadership group we have, groups we have in society. If they do not give a clear trumpet call, then there is no trumpet in the land and only an uncertain sound. And so that one can learn. And certainly one of the reasons for the performance of, let's say, Germany, Japan, has been the fact that in those countries the leadership group, not just in business, but above all in business, sees itself as representative and as being responsible for thinking through major policy decisions in areas of their competence. It is very hard in Germany to say whether the Bundesbank and the Ministry of Finance think through policies or the large German commercial banks, because they don't see themselves as separate in that sense. They say, who in our group knows most about this? And he may work for the Western Bank or for the Federal Bank, but he's one of us. And that is a very important difference. And you cannot import it into a system that, like our system, is based on checks and balances and on very careful, long-length relationships, and still how does it fit us? Believe me, I think we have reached the limits of the purely adversary process if we haven't exceeded it. And sometimes I feel that there's nothing wrong with a republic that's closing its law schools for 10 years, wouldn't cure, but it's not going to happen. But we have reached the limits of what one can hope to achieve by purely adversary processes. There is need for integrating leadership again. The second thing, let me say, is when you look at the economies that have done best, It is not the economies that, as all Keynesian dominated ones have been doing, started out with a domestic economy. Let me say, you all believe that there is a great deal of difference between Keynes and Milton Friedman, and if you permit my saying so, there is none. Both are macroeconomists. Both believe that the economist philosopher can control. both believe in demand economics and both believe, above all, in the supremacy of the domestic economy. All of these, I submit, have been disproven by the events of the last 30 years. And I think Friedman is a little more obsolete than the Keynesians because he's a little more doctrinaire. But that's a bland, that's a rather, I know some Canadians who can compete, and not, but, so, and believe me, if you look at the successful ones, these, by sheer accident, in one case, the Germans, and because of Irving Friedman and the others, the Japanese, did not start out this domestic economy. You see, very few people realize that the father of the Japanese miracle has the most un-Japanese name of Irving Friedman, and who in 1950 told the Japanese not to listen to the American economists, but to practically start out with the world economy rather than the domestic one. And the successful businesses as well as the successful economies of the last 30 years have accepted the fact that there is a world economy. It's a dreadfully complicated one. Irving said we have one currency, the euro dollar, but that's really saying we ain't got no currency, you know. In a way, we have, because the euro, not euro-dollar, as the standard of value is not terribly satisfactory just now, and nobody controls it and everybody tries to, and it's a muddle. But still, there is a world economy with its own dynamics and the dynamics lie in the world economy and bluntly, practically all domestic national policies of the last 20 years have been disastrous failures and only where the cue was taken from the world economy have you seen results. And the lesson to learn from others is that one starts out with the world economy, even if one is primarily domestic. Very few people know that next to the United States, the Japanese are least dependent on the world economy. No more than one-tenth of their gross national product comes out of their foreign transactions. 90% is domestic, and only the United States is less dependent. Every European country is far more dependent on the world economy, and yet the Japanese, again out of a mixture of intelligence and superstition, have always seen themselves as totally dependent on the world economy, which they are not, but as a result have been steered by the world economy and sought out with the question, what's going on outside Japan, and not with the question, what's going on inside. Even though they are just as conscious of the next election, even though every Japanese electoral district is a swing district, though they are not hampered as much as we are by laws forbidding bribery in politics so they can occasionally still make policy and then buy support for it which may not be a bad idea and at least it works occasionally but they start out with the question what goes on outside and that is something over which we have no control and that we therefore have to use as an opportunity or as something to adapt to. And I think increasingly we will have to learn this even though our market is so much larger, twice the Japanese at least, and even though the country is so much larger, about in territory maybe 15 times the size of Japan, and even though we are so heterogeneous as against the extreme homogeneity of Japan. We will still, I think, increasingly have to learn to understand a very complex and very fast-moving world economy. The third thing to learn is what marketing means. You know, we invented the term, and I know by now no company that doesn't preach it, but I'm not sure that I know many that practice it. Marketing is above all a structural concept. It is thinking through the structure of the outside. And now it's becoming popular in this country, the Boston Consulting Group concept, to say you have to have market leadership. It gives you disproportionate profitability. Ladies and gentlemen, the evidence does not support that theory. The evidence supports that that market position that fits the market gives you disproportionate returns. But that isn't leadership necessarily. That's leadership, yes, when the automobile industry of the world somehow, and we don't know why, turned from a series of national markets into a world market, then the Chrysler strategy became a strategy for losing, and this isn't hindsight. Some of us who know that industry said so in 1960, the strategy of being a number three in the national market and satisfying the rest of the world. Then one had to be one of probably no more than four or five world-class companies or a true specialist. There was Royce, a checker cab, a jeep, what have you. And in between, there was only wasteland. and that but when you're a book publisher you know that's a meaningless strategy if only because of the language barrier there isn't going to be world publishing how many of you are ever going to be able to read Chinese I won't I know that and secondly the book in book publishing is a very different industry because not one of us and I say that with my close friend and publisher in this room now not one of us has ever bought the book because that's the publisher's name on it we buy it for all kinds of reasons but not because it is an xyz book even though no publisher likes to hear it publishers in that sense are marketers and middlemen and not producers and though like any really good merchant they rightly dictate what is being produced to a large extent because they understand the market and bring it back to the producers who like all producers have no feel for the market no author understands the audience because he writes for himself if he is any good and so like any really good producer who produces basically for himself and uses his own standards and should or there is no commitment to the printer product but the only book publishing industry market leadership in terms of volume is not the most profitable course a market leadership in terms of a certain image, of a certain value concept. Yes, that's different. And when you go to cosmetics, volume is largely irrelevant. And you have a market that divides by very different value concepts. But this is marketing. And let me say, we preached it and we are not practicing it. We are still practicing selling basically and when you look at the Japanese but look also now one can look at these the best examples of marketing I know are the small family-owned Italian companies with 180 employees who are selling their products every place today they're the most successful entrepreneurs today despite all attempts by the Italian government to kill them off and systematically they are too small you know, basically what the Italian government is doing is trying to kill the mosques by throwing moss balls at them and you don't hit many mosques that way and those small people in Russia and Bergamo and what have you, who market specialty products

Thank you very much, Bill Dill. Ladies and gentlemen, let me first say once more how grateful I am and delighted to be allowed back to what, after all these years, is still very much my home, and how very much I appreciate that I am still being permitted to come here every year and to be a member of the faculty and of the school for a few short days. And usually, and I think I credit this to the GBA management, the weather is perfect. And let me say a welcome to all the many old friends I see in the audience. I hope I'll get around to saying a few words to each of you in the course of the day. But, quesamissio, let me say how happy I am to see so many people who have been friends of this school and of this lecture series and of myself for so many years. And I want to say in particular how grateful I am to Earth Crystal to take time out from what must easily be the busiest schedule in the nation next to Mr. Carter's. to be here and unlike Mr. Carter despite the hostages coming out and to be here with us because really this is his topic far more than mine and most of what I know about the topic I've really learned from reading Professor Crystal over the years and he has enlightened, really given all of us a new perspective on the political process and on the changes in the political environment.

and one would really be in terms of a political philosopher asking the question what has become of the modern national state of that proudest child of the modern age, which is clearly in an advanced stage of senility, premature senility, irreversible, I'm afraid. Or one can look and see, since one has to operate in what is and not in what was or in what should be or in what will be, what does it look like today? And I thought the intelligent topic for this session is not the philosophical one in which one tries to discern why modern government has become both obese and incompetent, But in which one looks at the situation and says, if you have to run an institution, a business today, what are the rules that no longer apply? What are the rules that sometimes apply? And what are the new rules that again only sometimes apply? because I think one of the characteristics of this period is that there are no rules that one can use with even high probability. And if you look at the situation and the way of crystal is going to, I think, stress other aspects of the same situation, And two things, or three, two certainly, strike me as being of particular importance and usually not seen by the executive in business. Let me say the greatest danger in turbulent times like ours is not the turbulence. The greatest danger is that you act rationally in terms of yesterday. and that you assume that the things that have worked for so long and we have been through the longest period of continuity in economic history ever recorded from 1950 or 48 until the early 70s and then one comes to believe that the things that worked in that period were really laid down on Mount Sinai, if not in the first six days of creation, and our laws of the Lord and laws of nature, whereas they were very temporary and transitory phenomena. And then one doesn't look, one reacts to a reality that no longer really prevails. And so I want to point out two things which most of my friends in businesses, especially top management in large businesses, who are very insulated, as I think you all know, take for granted and which simply are at least not solid anymore. The first is a structure of the population in which there was a constituency for business, a business constituency that in a way began with the owner of the corner cigar store and consisted of individuals who had a stake in business. And when you read the rhetoric of business leadership, including the Business Mount Table, for which I have great respect, and when you look at the lobbyists and so on, they all still assume this. And then one has to say very bluntly that there is no such constituency and that, in fact, no group in American society is as alienated, to use a nice, fashionable term, from big business. And what big business is, is a very debatable question. Believe me, it isn't just GM. The companies which you consider small business are seen as big business. Anything over a few hundred employees or 500 employees or so, where it just sees itself in terms of management and marketing and finance is big business. And the cigar store owner or his replacement, the fellow who owns five supermarkets in Portland, Oregon, does not see any identity either of point of view or of concerns or of perspective with them. There's a very sharp break and it is simply a result in large fact, a large measure of the fact that ownership of big business is not in the hands of individuals but in the hands of intermediaries

in number, small business sector, which large business sees as its normal conservative constituency. And really the two do not share their same concerns, they don't see the same world very much. And in a way the emergence of the intermediary intermediary as the vehicle through which capital is being formed, such as we form, we don't form enough, and in which savings are channeled into investment, is in many ways both inevitable and a great triumph. But it has resulted in a different political constituency. And one of the oldest proverbs of politics, going back all the way to Aristotle, is that Power follows property and power therefore is following in the sense that the employees who are the beneficiaries of these intermediaries one way or another are really in a new relationship to big business. On the one hand, we have the big business society and economy that is intimately related to the employees, their pension plans, their savings. And then we have a small business society which is related economically to big business, but not socially or psychologically or emotionally or even in terms of direct interest. And so the constituency is gone, and big business so far has not even tried to mobilize a new constituency. And I add to this the fact that most of you in management still see in your mind's eye the employee of 1920. You know, you open a management book, including mine, and read the discussion about labor relations and personnel management, and it is very clear that there are projections of what we learned in the early 20s in Detroit or in Pittsburgh. And that is not the employee of today, even in Detroit or in Pittsburgh. Even the dropout of today is a very different worker from the same steel worker of 1920. When I first knew the automobile industry, General Motors has just made the first educational survey of its supervisors, that was 1930, and the General Motors supervisor was 50 years old and therefore born in 1880 and he had at most two half-terms of formal schooling. And now I think you have a major problem, how to mobilize the new constituency in an employee society in which 95% or 92% of all national product goes out in the form of wages and salaries, and most of the rest is self-employed and doesn't profit either. and in which the only real source of capital formation, I do not believe that we will see a resurgence of personal saving, no matter what the tax laws are, simply because most of us feel that we are saving through the intermediaries. That's the first point. And the second point is that in all developed countries, and not just in this, the old integrative mechanisms to create a basis for action in the political arena is at best running on one cylinder with five cylinders kind of sputtering. That's the beginning of our history as a nation. It's a great debate over the danger of factionalism. And as an answer to it, we invented the political party. The political party is fundamentally an American invention and perhaps the most lasting legacy of James Madison as a very great political philosopher, which was the answer to faction, in which factions were brought together, united behind a goal such the election of a president or a majority in the Congress so that they were forced to submerge factional, which always means single cause interests, into a program. And we did it non-ideologically, always a kind of... Our parties were a one percent tincture of ideology. Anti-Europeans with about a 25% ideological content. The European parties were always far more interest parties than they were supposed to be. But they used common slogans, ideological slogans, to bring about a long coalition of interests. And if you are interested in that part of the history of ideas, that is, the history of political parties, you will see how skillful the 19th century was. Perhaps the last ones built on the old basis were still the European social democratic parties. And what has happened, let me say, is that this worked too well. It reached the point at which essentially the original designers of parties aim, where you had consensus in society. And as a result, the party no longer does its job. It used to be in American politics that a landslide was a president elected by more than 60% of the vote. A landslide today is a president elected by 50.1% of the vote. Every single electoral district has become a swing district. When I moved up to Vermont in 1942 and went to register, a very nice lady in North Pennington said, won't you register as a Democrat? And I said, why? And she said, we need a few respectable Democrats here. But six years later, when I was going to be in San Francisco at the Dewey Truman election and went down for an absentee ballot, she said, I can mail one to you, you can fill one out here, or I can put it in the Republican box for you myself. That was Vermont. That is no longer true. Even Vermont is a swing district, even Mississippi. And when you have nothing but 50% districts, in which there is no majority, then the small splinter group, the faction, acquires veto powers. And all during the 19th century, the Women's Christian Temperance Union tried to use the 3 to 5 to 8% of the voted command to force candidates to accept temperance, accept prohibition, and it never got any place because very few districts were so evenly balanced that a 5% veto could swing the election. And in 1918, as you know, it came to pass. And then the same year or two later, you had in India a very small group, which Gandhi mobilized, basically brought the world's greatest power of the time to its knees, because England by that time had become evenly balanced. And that lesson now has become accepted and understood by everybody. And so very small factional groups commanding microscopic fractions, sprinters of the vote, have a veto power. They cannot produce action, but they can block action. Dean Dill talked about Business Day. I think the active support for Business Day is probably one-tenth or one percent if it's that large. And yet that is large enough in some areas to block. And so the parties have lost their power to integrate a majority and are becoming the victims of factions. And if you want to read what this means, the best text on it is still the Federalist Papers, where they were so conscious of that danger and of the fact that this would paralyze the political process and would make impossible any action for a program that basically thinks through priorities, That basically decides at what point one balances one desirable good against another, that in other words can establish political action. And that induces then the paralysis we have now.

And finally, at one point, going on for nine years, I had really—I had told the idea to them, thinking, it's there, baby, let them run with it. And so I wrote to Harold Williams, and I said, I want an official opinion. I know Harold. I said, I want an official opinion from you. Is there an SEC problem in this or not? And Harold Williams sent it around to his staff, and he sent me a very legalistic document. Turns out there's no SEC problem at all with differential stock dividends. There may be problems at the state level with state legislation. If there are such problems, and even then, no one seems to be quite sure, but they're easily solved. Why shouldn't they let corporations do that if corporations want to do it? The sad truth, and I have come to this conclusion most reluctantly, is that the reason it isn't happening is not because it's difficult, not because there are legal hurdles, because the last thing in the world that CEOs want is an active, concerned, interested stockholder constituency. I think, I suppose, a CEO, every night before he goes to sleep, has many nightmares. One of them would be to wake up in the morning and find his office full of stockholders. And this is so, and it's understandable. It's like a professor waking up in the morning and findings house full of students. I mean, we have those nightmares too. But in the end, if you take seriously your role as a part of a political faction or as a political faction contending with other political factions, you have to take seriously the responsibility of organizing your potential strength. And it seems to me sad and negligent that corporations should have failed to explore this idea more seriously than they have, because I do think that over a period of time, it would be very, very useful to them. I also think there's so many other things that corporations can and should do. I don't think, and here I disagree, I have to say I really disagree with Peter. I don't want to see American corporations sit down with Peter Drucker or with me or anybody and say, don't tell us what's good for the corporation. Tell us what we should do

incapacity to understand politics well, because in business, the whole mode of business is different from the mode of politics. Business is a decision-making activity, practical activity of a decision-making kind. It doesn't matter whether decision-making is hierarchical or consensual, but it's a decision-making activity. Politics is not a decision-making activity. It's an activity in which you rarely get the opportunity or the pleasure of making a decision. Most of the time, it is a negotiating activity, which is, incidentally, why lawyers tend to be quite good at it and have played such a prominent role in modern democratic politics. I think that corporations coping with this new environment and this environment that will persist for quite a while, really have to think of changing, of not only trying to secure a solid base with a vested interest in the corporations, and I don't think the pension funds will provide that because the pension funds involved in the corporation is consistent with any kind of management of the corporation, and it's consistent with socialized corporations, with Ralph Nades corporations as well as the ones that exist. And I really am most interested in a corporation as a bulwark of a free society. Even the least admirable corporations are that, just as I agree, I think the proliferation of churches and religious institutions in this society are bulwarks of a free society. I don't agree with all of them, obviously. I only agree with one. And I don't even like some of them. But never mind. The fact that they're there is very important. And the fact that they exist as independent centers of power is very important. Therefore, I think it's very important that corporations continue to exist as independent sources of power. For this to happen, however, vested interests will have to be created. I think corporate leadership is going to be attentive to anything. I think it should be more attentive to small business. Without the buttressing of small business, small business has the political strength. You want to get something through Congress, don't go to the top CEOs. Go to those local undertakers, those local druggists, those local, you forgot one very important small business group, those local automobile dealers. Not this year, perhaps. But the richest man in town is usually the local automobile dealer, not the plant manager of a major factory. These are the people with influence. These are the people who are the business establishment in local communities, and they are the important ones. If business leaders find that difficult to do, corporate leaders, then go for a stockholder constituency. In addition, of course, there is the whole question of how you communicate with other factions in society or with other potential allies or potential adversaries. I really think business communications are an absolutely terrible state, largely because they have been handled mainly by personal relations, which are out of date, as Peter says, or by public relations, which is not the name of the game today. Public relations is an activity whereby you try to persuade journalists to think well of you. Not a very productive activity at the moment. And it was only a productive activity when journalists didn't care what they wrote about business. It's only a productive activity when journalists and publishers were bribed by business, to put it very bluntly. The corporation has to have a sense of its communications with its employees. Corporations don't share problems with employees. Very interesting. They boast of their accomplishment, but corporate leadership, corporate management, hates sharing problems with anyone, including, of course, stockholders. It's interesting. I've been interested in the automobile situation. Now, American automobile companies really have been disadvantaged by government regulations vis-a-vis the foreign imports. There's just no question about that, all sorts of government regulations. But at no point that I have been able to determine has the management of corporations been going down to their workers and saying, look, this is the problem, and explaining in great detail why we're not doing well. I don't believe Chrysler ever did that to its employees, explaining why we're having the problems we're having. I don't expect them to confess their sins of lousy management. That would be too much to expect. But at least to explain why the government regulations were having that particular impact upon Chrysler. I don't believe there was any effort to communicate to employees in that way. Corporate leaders don't like communicating problems, but communicating problems are what really is interesting. No one's interested in just success stories. Problems, particularly if they're gonna affect your life and your job and your career, are very interesting indeed. I mean, I don't understand why drug companies aren't explaining to their employees some of the problems they have with the Food and Drug Administration. They shouldn't, people should know this. And similarly with every industry, all of which has enormous problems with foreign competition perhaps, but always with government, no effort is made to, I won't even use the word educate, but just simply to inform their employees in a continuous way about the problems the business is facing. So suddenly, when things go bad, everyone is not surprised, and being surprised becomes very suspicious of what is going on. No point in communicating this with the union leadership. You want to communicate it with the employees. And the last point I wish to make involves the relationship of these corporate leaders who, as I agree, are here to stay, heads of major organizations, with the most powerful community in our society, namely the intellectual and academic community. The situation is improving, but very, very slowly, in part because even today your average CEO doesn't understand how important the intellectual and academic communities are, though I have begun to get through to them now by saying, look, what do you have vis-a-vis the academic community? You have money. You can ring up a senator, and he'll probably return your call. You have influence of that kind. But they have hostages. They've got your children as hostages. You know, when we have a situation today, when I would wager half the children of the chief executive's offices of this country despise business or have a low opinion of business as an activity, you begin to wonder, how in God's name is business going to communicate? How is it going to successfully defend the business system? And the answer is that in a war between the business and academic communities, the academic community will always win. It may lose a temporary battle. It'll always win the war in the long run because it has the children. They own the children, yours and mine. And so this gulf that exists between the academic intellectual community on the one hand and the business community on the other is tragic. Efforts must be made to bridge it on both sides. I have no great illusions as to how easy it's going to be, but it's very difficult. And you run into all sorts of difficulties. You run into the difficulty that business executives are too busy to read, and being too busy to read, their intellectual muscles atrophy. Not their analytical muscles, they're still perfectly good, competent at analyzing a problem very cogently, but their intellectual muscles, which are not the same thing as analytical muscles, intellectual muscles being the muscle which permits you to play with an idea, to entertain it, speculate about it, think about it, not necessarily come to a conclusion about it right away, not in a decision-making context. I don't really know what to do about this, except that I do think that larger corporations are going to have to somehow internalize their knowledge, the attitudes, not necessarily the attitudes, the knowledge and expertise of the academic and intellectual milieu. They really need, they've got to somehow learn what's happening in that world, learn to appreciate in that world, have people fairly high up who read it, who read what's written in that world. I'll take a test right now. I assume the majority of you are business executives. How many of you subscribe to the New Republic? How many of you subscribe to Commentary? You don't know what's happening in the world. It's true, you really don't. That's where the future is being shaped. It's where your future is being shaped, and not necessarily in those two magazines, though I think I picked the two best, the one slightly right of center, one slightly left of center, but in magazines of that kind. Somehow or other, the corporation has to have links with that other world of action, the world of ideas where your future and mine, I guess, will be shaped. Well, I could go on indefinitely, but it's time for the break. And I can't go on indefinitely. I could go on for a while. But it's time for the break. And one reason for this is not that the structures have become so much more complex, but that we have neglected the second approach to, what, to call it to governance, which is traditional. the last 30 years you know if you look at the history of political theory and basically when we talk organization structure we are talking governance and political theory there are two strands in western the western tradition one is the constitutionalist one which basically says what are the right laws so that even mediocre people can function and so that the evildoers are at least confined and the other one which went by the name of the education of the christian prince so it also goes back to the greeks and before says how do we form the rulers so that even if If there are turbulent times and the rules aren't clear, we get the best there is and we get virtue into the system and leadership. And in the last 30 years we have emphasized the constitutional approach. Let me say this is normally in this country where business basically started out taking its structural concepts from the American Constitution. If you look at our organization theory, it is tremendously influenced by the Constitution, for better or worse, largely for better, because at least it preaches the need to think through the limitations of power, but not entirely. It's no longer true, as it was in the 50s, that researchers were so badly paid in Germany or Austria or Japan that they only too gladly took that job in Peoria. They don't anymore. One of the things to learn about managing anything is when to abandon. This is also a chapter heading in managing the boss. When do you abandon a boss? There is still no better prescription for success than to have a boss who is going and no more certain prescription for frustration and failure than to work for an incumbent. If you overreach the boss in the sense that the things that are right, he's just unwilling, unable, incapable of grasping and of doing, you have an incompetent boss. And then that is one of the few cases where I would always counsel in favor of exchange, a transfer, change in jobs. And the other one is a corrupt boss. And I don't mean one who dips his hands into the till. That's one form of corruption. But the most serious form of corruption is one who has values, standards, that are ethically and morally unacceptable to you, that just demean you. One does not ask because one will become corrupt oneself. One will become contemptuous of oneself. One will begin to lose oneself. So if you work for an incompetent or for a corrupt boss, get out. If you find yourself in a position in which you have gotten as much out of the job, out of the boss, out of the work, as it will ever give you, and you are still below late middle age, you are still concerned with where am I going to go, who am I going to be, what opportunities do I have, Then one moves out. Then one says, all right, I've gotten everything out of this company, this work, this boss. It's likely to give me, and I've given as much as I'm likely to give, and now it's time for me to move on. You know, Elizabeth, in my work, I write a great many reports. I see a great many reports. I would say that the typical management report I see is the last draft and not the final document. People think that when they understand understand a subject matter. They have done their writing job. That, as any professional writer can tell them, is when the writing job becomes possible. Then one sits down and says, now I understand what I'm talking about, and now I have to think through whom I am talking to. One of the oldest rules is that logic comes first, but then comes rhetoric, the art of effectiveness. And reports are written to be effective. What most reports need to be effective management tools is that last go-around. It need not take much time. One says, what are we trying to accomplish with whom? This report goes to the executive committee. What are the things that are important to them? How can they act on it? And how can we tell them what we expect to come out of this? And there we can learn from the military. In the military, this is being taught. After you have done your staff work, you sit down and write the covering letter, which has one question. Who is going to read it and what is he expected to do with it? How do we tell him? The military and system is being one page all right. I think that's not a bad rule, but one doesn't have to be that pedantic. Make it four if you have an executive committee that likes to read, a good many of them do. Concern yourself with the effectiveness of the report, because by itself it will be literature and not action.

I indeed do. I think the two are two very different things and lead to very different conclusions. One has to start out with a fairly clear idea of what performance is expected. The typical performance appraisal that says, how do you rate him from outstanding to no damn good without ever telling you what performance is, is silly. because there are no outstanding people, there are no poor people. Good for what? One cannot appraise performance by itself. One can only appraise performance against a pre-established, reasonably clear target. Then you say, this is what we planned to do and this is what we did, and in this area we did something quite different from what we had planned to do and it was the right thing to do. We learned something on the job. In this area, we did so much worse than we had expected to do, and in this one we did better. One learns and feeds back from a performance appraisal on defining performance and task again. But when it comes to the performer, one says, what has this person done well? I may be much too dogmatic and rigid in never permitting myself to talk about potential of people. I consider that obscene almost, and silly. I have for 35 years or so kind of watched, and there is no correlation between potential and performance. Believe me, neither positive nor negative. When you appraise a performer, you are trying to look for strength, trying to understand capacity. When you look for performance, you are looking for accomplishment.

Any organization, like any organism, has to have a process of elimination or else the toxic waste poisons the whole system.
